hero.headline: An AI software agency where every worker has its own brain.
hero.subheadline: 66 AI workers in 12 divisions, each with its own model and plugins. One command starts them on your own machine.

stats.heading: AMORA in numbers
stats.statement: AMORA runs *66* workers across *12* divisions. Models plug in *4* ways, and no task gets more than *3* tries before it comes back to you.

pillars.heading: What makes it more than a prompt library
pillars.intro: Three things a folder of prompts cannot do on its own.

items.title: The rules live in code
items.body: A plain-code orchestrator owns the task queue, the quality gates, the retries, and the budget. Models help plan and review, but none of them can argue past a failing test or a spending limit.

items.title: Each worker has its own model
items.body: The Slice / Markup Engineer reads screenshots, so it gets a model with vision. The Task Dispatcher hands out tasks all day, so it gets something cheap and fast.

items.title: Every handoff is on record
items.body: When one worker passes work to the next, AMORA logs the contract, whether it validated, the gate result, which model answered, and what it cost.

steps.title: You write a brief
steps.body: Type the job into the dashboard the way you'd explain it to a colleague. Attach designs or specs, set a budget, and choose whether you sign off at every gate or only at the end.

steps.title: You approve the plan
steps.body: The Planner / Decomposer in Nexus shows which workers it wants and in what order. Nothing runs until you approve it, so a bad plan costs nothing.

steps.title: Divisions pick it up
steps.body: Compass works out the scope, Atelier designs it, and Forge builds it, each worker on its own model.

steps.title: Dev and QA go back and forth
steps.body: Crucible tests what Forge builds, and failures go back to the developer. After three attempts the task stops and comes to you instead of looping forever.

steps.title: The Gatekeeper checks it
steps.body: Lint, type checks, tests, and visual diffs run as code. When something fails you get the reason, like "Visual diff 4.2%, limit 3%".

steps.title: You approve the result
steps.body: The diff waits in the dashboard with an Approve button. If you've connected Telegram, a summary with the same two buttons reaches your phone.

dashboard.heading: Decisions first, then everything else
dashboard.intro: Running amora opens a dashboard on your own machine. What's waiting on you sits at the top, followed by what's running and what it's costing.

features.title: A plan before any spend
features.body: Every task starts with a plan preview. No worker touches it until you approve who does what.

features.title: Every handoff, inspectable
features.body: Open a task to see each handoff with its contract, validation result, gate result, the model that answered, and the cost.

features.title: Budgets that actually stop work
features.body: Set limits per task and per day. When one is hit, dispatching stops until you decide what happens next.

features.title: One button stops everything
features.body: Pause all workers sits on every page. Queued work stops, task state is kept, and Resume picks up where it left off.

approval.text: Pricing page is ready for review

divisions.heading: Meet the 12 divisions
divisions.intro: Each division is named after a room in the agency's headquarters. Open a row to see who works there.
divisions.waveLegend: Workers ship in three waves: 29 in the first, 20 in the second, and the last 17 in the third.

brains.heading: What's inside a worker
brains.intro: Each worker is a manifest file. Point its model slot at whatever you like. AMORA probes the model and refuses the change when it can't do the job.

anatomy.body: A slot, not a model name. It resolves from global to division to worker, so you can change one worker without touching the rest. Fallbacks have to meet the same requirements.
What the model must support, like vision or tool use. AMORA probes for each one and rejects a model that misses any.
Capabilities the worker needs, like design_source. Figma, Penpot, or a folder of images can each provide it.
Typed input and output, like design_spec.v1, so the next worker knows exactly what it's getting.
Which files it can touch, which commands it can run, and whether it can reach the network.

demo.heading: Try giving a worker the wrong model
demo.sameFamily: Same base family as {model}, which the {worker} uses. A reviewer has to come from a different family.
demo.differentFamily: Different base family from {model}, which the {worker} uses.

telegram.heading: Approvals follow you to Telegram
telegram.intro: It's optional. Paste a bot token into the dashboard's settings, and each division gets its own topic in your group. You hear about a task when it changes state, and you get a button when it needs you. The diffs, handoffs, and keys stay in the dashboard.

install.heading: Install
install.intro: One command starts the runtime and opens the dashboard in your browser, where a short setup gets you to your first task. You'll need Node.js and a key for at least one model gateway. Docker is optional and only sandboxes the code workers run.
install.notice: [PLACEHOLDER] The package isn't published yet. These commands follow the spec until the first release.
install.setupHeading: What the first run asks you

setup.title: Connect a gateway
setup.body: OmniRoute by default, or OpenRouter, a provider directly, or local models through Ollama. The key goes into your OS keychain.

setup.title: Check your models
setup.body: AMORA tests each model for tool use, structured output, and vision. A model that fails a check a worker needs can't be given to that worker.

setup.title: Pick your workers
setup.body: Wave 1 is switched on: 29 workers, enough to plan, design, build, and test a web feature. Add more waves later.

setup.title: Set a budget
setup.body: A limit per task and per day. No task starts without one.

setup.title: Connect Telegram, if you want
setup.body: Paste the bot token here, never in a chat. You can skip this and add it later in Settings.

commands.body: Checks your keys, plugins, model capabilities, and hardware.
Shows which worker uses which model.
Shows what you've spent with each provider.
Runs the dashboard on a port you choose.

security.heading: Your keys stay on your machine

items.title: Keys live in your OS keychain
items.body: Keychain on macOS, Credential Manager on Windows, Secret Service on Linux. The dashboard only ever shows the last four characters, and keys never go through Telegram.

items.title: The dashboard only listens on 127.0.0.1
items.body: Every request needs the session from your one-time sign-in link, and requests from other websites are turned away. Nothing loads from third-party hosts.

items.title: Handoffs are scanned for secrets
items.body: A secret scanner reads every handoff before it's written to disk, and keys are never written to logs.

items.title: Plugins ask before they get access
items.body: Each plugin lists the folders and network access it wants. You approve them before it's switched on.

items.title: Code can run in a sandbox
items.body: Turn on Docker and workers execute code in an isolated container instead of directly on your computer.

finalCta.heading: Try it on a small project first
finalCta.body: AMORA is open source and still experimental. Bring your own model keys and set a budget before the first task.
